bridge: I04 introduced independent tool checks and D07 introduced test fixtures. Use local mocks and fixed inputs, with no live scoring or provider calls.
teaching:
### State the property to check

Examples include “one account cannot retrieve another account's record” and “a request cannot exceed the configured work limit”. Give each property an enforcement point and observable outcome.

### Use fixed positive and negative cases

A permitted lookup should succeed. A cross-account lookup should fail before private content is exposed. Repeated requests should not bypass quotas or duplicate a write. A fixture supplies a known input and expected result so the control can be tested directly.

### Bound the work

Limit request size, context size, concurrent jobs, tool calls, time and output where relevant. Check cancellation and failure paths too. An expensive loop can come from ordinary faulty behaviour as well as malicious intent.

### Keep test claims proportionate

Offline mocks can establish application logic under controlled responses. They do not establish a model's real behaviour, latency or broad attack resistance. Keep any later authorised provider study separate, with its own scope and cost controls.

### Plan ongoing operation

Identify what configuration or dependency changes would require rechecking the controls. Record failures and residual risk rather than converting a checklist into a blanket safety certificate.
example:
Static executor cases (expected)
A read A1 within grant -> allow
A read B1             -> deny ownership
A send email          -> deny unavailable tool
A read A1 after budget exhausted -> deny budget
Missing principal     -> deny authentication
Known harmless task success -> required positive case
No model invocation or inference scoring is needed.
explanation: The table verifies a policy implementation if later translated into isolated mocked unit tests; it does not measure what a model would propose. Keep that distinction in any report. Removing the positive case would allow a deny-everything implementation to appear secure while unusable.
exercise: Hand-check all six cases and write a verification plan identifying the assertion owner, inputs and expected observable result. Define max input bytes, tool count, duration and retry count for a fictional task, without executing a run.
solution: Example paper limits for a fictional read-only task: at most 8,000 UTF-8 input bytes, 3 tool calls, a 10-second overall deadline and 1 retry within that same budget. These illustrative caps need workload-specific validation before deployment. Allowed own-document read succeeds; foreign-document read denies ownership; send denies unavailable tool; exhausted-budget read denies budget; missing principal denies authentication; the known harmless task must succeed under available budget. The executor owns those checks and returns a bounded failure outcome when a limit is reached. The paper table does not execute an implementation or measure model robustness.
challenge: Critique “the agent passed 100 safety prompts, therefore it is secure.” State missing threat-model/coverage information and design a bounded offline policy check that adds useful evidence without any live evaluation.
challenge_solution: Need authorised scope, attack surfaces, data, action limits, distributions and failure analysis. Offline guarded-executor cases can establish selected enforcement behaviour; they cannot justify a universal model-security claim. Keep the live workload paused until explicitly authorised.
